heroIntro: Purchasing a residential apartment in Dhaka, Chittagong, or other urban centers represents a lifetime investment for local buyers and non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs). However, one of the most widespread grievances in the housing sector is project delay. Real estate developers routinely promise completion within thirty-six to forty-eight months, but buyers frequently find their projects stalled for five to ten years while builders divert funds to subsequent commercial ventures. Under the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (রিয়েল এস্টেট উন্নয়ন ও ব্যবস্থাপনা আইন, ২০১০), developers do not enjoy unlimited discretion. The law establishes strict statutory compensation requirements for every month of delay under Section 15, alongside criminal prosecution and imprisonment under Section 24 for fraudulent builders.

quickAnswer.title: What Can You Do If a Developer Delays Apartment Handover in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Under Section 15 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010, if a developer fails to hand over an apartment by the contractual completion date, the developer is legally obligated to pay the purchaser agreed monthly compensation (or reasonable rental compensation) for every month of delay. If the developer completely fails to complete the building or you choose to cancel the contract, Section 15(2) mandates a full refund of all deposited money plus interest within sixty (60) days. If the developer refuses to pay, demands unauthorized extra charges, or sells the flat to another buyer, you can initiate statutory arbitration under Section 36 or file a criminal prosecution before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate under Sections 24, 27, and 28 of the Act, which carries imprisonment up to three years or fines up to 20 Lakh BDT.
highlights: Developers are legally mandated to pay monthly delay compensation under Section 15 of the 2010 Act.
Purchasers have the statutory right to cancel and demand full refund with interest.
Building deviations violating approved RAJUK/CDA plans are punishable criminal offences.
Defaulting developers face criminal imprisonment up to 3 years and heavy fines under Section 24.

sections.title: 1. The Statutory Framework: Developer Obligations under the 2010 Act
sections.content:
For years, real estate builders in Bangladesh operated in an unregulated environment, exploiting one-sided, boilerplate buyer agreements. In 2010, the government enacted the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (Act No. XLVIII of 2010) to protect flat buyers, establish building safety, and eliminate rogue real estate entities.

Under Section 5 of the Act, no developer can launch, market, or advertise a real estate project without obtaining formal registration from the government (RAJUK, CDA, KDA, RDA, or the National Housing Authority). Under Section 13, all terms of sale must be documented in a registered bilateral contract that clearly specifies the apartment unit, floor layout, parking allotment, total purchase price, installment breakdown, and the exact handover date.

Crucially, Section 13(2) prohibits developers from including arbitrary clauses that unilaterally relieve the builder of liability for delays. The statutory protections established in the 2010 enactment are mandatory; they cannot be overridden by fine-print contractual waivers.

sections.title: 2. Section 15 Delay Compensation: Monthly Rent Payments & Interest Calculations
sections.content:
The core economic protection for apartment purchasers is established in Section 15 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 ('Handover of Real Estate'). Under Section 15(1), the developer is legally bound to complete construction and hand over possession of the real estate, along with all promised common utilities, within the timeline specified in the contract.

If the developer fails to hand over the apartment within the contractual timeframe due to reasons within their control, Section 15(1) establishes that the developer must pay the purchaser compensation at the rate agreed upon in the contract for every month of delay. If the contract fails to stipulate a specific penalty rate, the developer must pay monthly compensation equivalent to the reasonable prevailing market rental value of the apartment.

This monthly compensation continues to accumulate for every single month until actual physical possession is delivered along with the completion certificate. Builders cannot escape this statutory compensation by claiming material price escalation or routine labor delays, as these represent standard commercial risks assumed by the developer.

sections.title: 3. Contract Cancellation & Full Refund with Statutory Interest (Section 15(2))
sections.content:
In numerous stalled projects, construction ceases completely, and the purchaser loses confidence that the developer will ever complete the building. In such circumstances, the buyer is not forced to wait indefinitely.

Under Section 15(2) of the Real Estate Act 2010, if the developer completely fails to complete the real estate or if the purchaser chooses to cancel the agreement due to prolonged, unauthorized delay, the purchaser is entitled to cancel the contract. The developer is statutorily mandated to refund the entire amount of money deposited by the purchaser, alongside interest at the prevailing commercial banking rate, within a maximum of sixty (60) days from the date of cancellation notice.

sections.title: 4. Building Plan Deviations: Section 14 Violations and Structural Alterations
sections.content:
A frequent malpractice among developers in Dhaka and Chittagong is deviating from approved architectural and structural plans. Builders often construct unauthorized additional floors, convert mandatory car parking into commercial shops, curtail common stairways, or reduce the net square footage of the purchased apartment.

Under Section 14 of the Real Estate Act 2010, the developer is strictly prohibited from making any structural alteration, layout modification, or utility change without the prior written consent of the purchaser and the formal approval of the planning authority (e.g., RAJUK under the Dhaka Building Construction Rules).

If a developer delivers an apartment with reduced square footage, Section 14(2) mandates that the developer must refund the proportionate value of the missing square footage, calculated at the original purchase rate, plus statutory interest. Constructing beyond approved height limits exposes the building to demolition notices, making plan verification an essential buyer safeguard.

sections.title: 5. Criminal Penalties: Jailing Fraudulent Builders under Sections 24, 27 & 28
sections.content:
The Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 is not merely a civil compensation statute; it contains teeth in the form of severe criminal punishments for defaulting builders.

Key penal provisions applicable against unscrupulous developers include:

  • Section 24 (Unauthorized Alteration / Delayed Handover Failure): Punishes developers who willfully fail to complete construction or alter approved plans without consent with imprisonment up to three (3) years, or a fine up to 20 Lakh BDT, or both.
  • Section 27 (Double Selling / Multiple Allocation): If a developer sells, mortgages, or transfers the same apartment unit to more than one purchaser, such fraudulent act is punishable with imprisonment up to three (3) years, or a fine up to 20 Lakh BDT, or both.
  • Section 28 (Unauthorized Commercial Charges): Imposes criminal penalties on builders who demand illegal extra fees or escalate agreed prices without contractual basis.

Criminal complaints under these sections are filed directly before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM), resulting in the immediate issuance of summons or arrest warrants against the Managing Director and directors of the developer enterprise.

sections.title: 7. Mandatory Arbitration Protocols under Section 36 of the 2010 Act
sections.content:
Under Section 36 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010, the legislature created an expedited dispute resolution framework: any dispute arising between a developer and a purchaser must initially be referred to amicable settlement and arbitration under the Arbitration Act 2001.

The purchaser serves a formal thirty-day statutory notice detailing the breach (e.g., accumulated handover delay compensation) and nominating an independent arbitrator. If the developer fails to respond, disputes the claim, or refuses to appoint an arbitrator within thirty days, Section 36(3) establishes that the dispute shall be resolved through judicial proceedings.

The buyer can then immediately file a civil suit before the Joint District Judge Court for recovery of the compensation or initiate criminal proceedings under Section 24 and Section 27 before the Magistrate Court. Furthermore, if the developer is an active member of the Real Estate and Housing Association of Bangladesh (REHAB), the buyer can file a formal complaint with the REHAB Mediation Committee to freeze the builder's membership standing.

sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Expatriate Flat Buyer Forcing Handover and 18 Lakh BDT Compensation
sections.content:
To illustrate how legal remedies unfold against defaulting builders, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

An expatriate physician residing in Manchester, UK, purchased a 2,200 sq. ft. luxury apartment in Gulshan, Dhaka, from a prominent real estate firm in 2019 for 3.5 Crore BDT. The registered agreement stipulated a handover date of December 2022, with an explicit delay penalty clause of 50,000 BDT per month. By mid-2025—thirty months past the deadline—the building remained an unpainted shell, while the developer demanded an additional 25 Lakh BDT citing construction material inflation.

The doctor engaged a Supreme Court property advocate in Dhaka. The advocate served a statutory legal notice under Section 15 and Section 36 of the Real Estate Act 2010, demanding immediate completion, rejecting the unauthorized price escalation, and claiming 15 Lakh BDT in accumulated delay compensation. When the builder ignored the notice, the advocate filed an emergency application for an injunction under Order 39 CPC, coupled with a criminal complaint under Section 24 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.

Faced with arrest warrants for its corporate directors and frozen marketing operations on the Gulshan project, the developer immediately negotiated a binding settlement (Solenama). The developer completed the apartment within four months, waived all unauthorized price escalation, and paid 18 Lakh BDT in accrued delay compensation, handing over the registered Saf Kabala deed.

sections.title: 9. Essential Contract Vetting Checklist for Prospective Apartment Buyers
sections.content:
Purchasers can avert years of agonizing litigation by conducting rigorous legal vetting before signing developer agreements in Bangladesh:

  • Verify RAJUK/CDA Project Approval: Never buy based on glossy brochures. Verify the original building approval letter, architectural layout plan, and structural clearance from the planning authority.
  • Inspect Landowner-Developer Joint Venture Deed: If the project is a joint venture (JV), examine the registered power of attorney given by the landowner to the developer to confirm the builder's legal authority to sell that specific apartment unit.
  • Ensure Strict Delayed Handover Penalty Clause: Ensure the agreement contains a specific monthly compensation figure (e.g., 50,000 to 100,000 BDT per month) and avoid ambiguous 'unforeseen delay' exceptions.
  • Avoid Cash Payments: Disburse all installment payments strictly through account-payee cheques, pay orders, or international bank transfers with detailed transaction descriptions.
  • Check REHAB & Ministry Registration: Confirm that the developer is formally registered under the Real Estate Act 2010 and holds active membership with REHAB.

faqs.question: What is the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010?
faqs.answer: The Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (Act No. XLVIII of 2010) is the primary statute in Bangladesh regulating real estate builders, protecting flat buyers, mandating handover timelines, and imposing criminal penalties for construction fraud.

faqs.question: Can I get compensation if a developer delays handing over my flat in Dhaka?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 15(1) of the Real Estate Act 2010, the developer is legally obligated to pay agreed monthly compensation or the prevailing market rental value for every month of delay beyond the contractual handover date.

faqs.question: Can I cancel my apartment contract and get a full refund if the project is stalled?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 15(2), if the developer fails to complete the building, the purchaser has the statutory right to cancel the agreement and demand a full refund of all deposited money plus bank interest within 60 days.

faqs.question: Can a real estate developer be jailed for delaying flat handover?
faqs.answer: Under Section 24 of the Real Estate Act 2010, developers who willfully fail to complete construction or deliver property without valid cause face criminal imprisonment for up to three years, or a fine up to 20 Lakh BDT, or both.

faqs.question: What should I do if a developer sells my booked flat to someone else?
faqs.answer: Double-selling an apartment is a grave criminal offence under Section 27 of the 2010 Act, punishable with up to three years imprisonment. You can file an immediate criminal CR case before the Magistrate and obtain an injunction.

faqs.question: Can a builder demand extra money above the agreed contract price?
faqs.answer: No. Under Section 13 and Section 28 of the Act, a developer cannot unilaterally escalate the purchase price unless explicitly provided for in a registered contract approved by the purchaser.

faqs.question: What is the role of REHAB in resolving developer-buyer disputes?
faqs.answer: If the developer is a member of REHAB, buyers can lodge formal mediation complaints. However, REHAB mediation is voluntary and does not prevent you from pursuing civil and criminal court remedies.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi buyer sue a developer without traveling to Dhaka?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas buyer can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, empowering an advocate in Dhaka to issue legal notices, initiate arbitration, and conduct court trials.
